discovery: Discovery of high-energy cosmic neutrinos and the founding of neutrino astronomy with large-volume ice Cherenkov telescopes
motivation: Halzen and Spiering turned the decades-old dream of a cubic-kilometre neutrino telescope into reality. Spiering pioneered deep-underwater and in-ice detection (Baikal, AMANDA) and shaped the European contribution, while Halzen conceived and led IceCube at the South Pole. In 2013 IceCube discovered a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at PeV energies, the first new window on the high-energy universe since gamma rays. This was followed by the multi-messenger identification of the blazar TXS 0506+056 (2018), evidence for neutrino emission from the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and the observation of neutrinos from the Galactic plane (2023). These results establish neutrinos as a working astronomical messenger that probes hadronic cosmic accelerators hidden from photons. The discovery rests on a bold detector concept, decades of patient engineering and data-taking, and robust statistics, and it has launched a new generation of observatories (KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD, IceCube-Gen2, P-ONE).
